claim: Two E3 ligases, BIG BROTHER (BB) and DA2, activate the latent peptidases DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 by mono-ubiquitination at multiple sites in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, two E3 ligases, BIG BROTHER (BB) and DA2, activate the latent peptidases DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 by mono-ubiquitination at multiple sites.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Dong et al., 2017) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Activated peptidases DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 destabilize various positive growth regulators.
source: Subsequently, these activated peptidases destabilize various positive growth regulators.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Dong et al., 2017) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Two ubiquitin-specific proteases, UBP12 and UBP13, deubiquitinate DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, reducing their peptidase activity.
source: Here, we show that two ubiquitin-specific proteases, UBP12 and UBP13, deubiquitinate DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, hence reducing their peptidase activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Overexpression of UBP12 or UBP13 strongly decreased leaf size and cell area.
source: Overexpression of UBP12 or UBP13 strongly decreased leaf size and cell area, and resulted in lower ploidy levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 2 and ploidy data in Figure 3.

claim: Overexpression of UBP12 or UBP13 resulted in lower ploidy levels.
source: Overexpression of UBP12 or UBP13 strongly decreased leaf size and cell area, and resulted in lower ploidy levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mutants in which UBP12 and UBP13 were downregulated produced smaller leaves that contained fewer and smaller cells.
source: Mutants in which UBP12 and UBP13 were downregulated produced smaller leaves that contained fewer and smaller cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic and cellular analysis data shown in Figure 2B-C for ubp12-2 mutants.

claim: Neither UBP12 nor UBP13 were found to be cleavage substrates of the activated DA1.
source: Remarkably, neither UBP12 nor UBP13 were found to be cleavage substrates of the activated DA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cleaving assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 work upstream of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 to restrict their protease activity.
source: Our results therefore suggest that UBP12 and UBP13 work upstream of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 to restrict their protease activity and hence fine-tune plant growth and development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including deubiquitination assays and genetic analyses.

claim: Ubiquitination plays a prominent role in the signaling cascades of many plant hormones including auxins, jasmonates, gibberellins, and strigolactones.
source: Ubiquitination plays a prominent role in the signaling cascades of many plant hormones (Santner and Estelle, 2010), such as auxins (Salehin et al., 2015), jasmonates (Nagels Durand et al., 2016), gibberellins (Wang and Deng, 2011), and strigolactones (Marzec, 2016), but also in many plant developmental processes and responses to stress (Shu and Yang, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The Arabidopsis genome codes for more than 1400 genes that encode E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: The tremendous diversity of the ubiquitination system and its potential in post-translational regulation are illustrated by the presence of more than 1400 genes that encode E3 ligases in Arabidopsis (Vierstra, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vierstra, 2009.

claim: The Arabidopsis genome codes for around 50 deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs).
source: The Arabidopsis genome codes for around 50 DUBs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: DUBs can be divided into five classes: ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolases (UHCs), JAB1/MPN/MOV34 (JAMM) domain DUBs, ovarian tumor proteases, Machado-Josephin domain (MJD) DUBs, and ubiquitin binding proteins (UBPs).
source: As in yeast and mammals, they can be divided into five classes: the ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolases (UHCs), JAB1/MPN/MOV34 (JAMM) domain DUBs that are zinc metalloproteases, ovarian tumor proteases, the Machado-Josephin domain (MJD) DUBs, and the ubiquitin binding proteins (UBPs), which is the largest group (Isono and Nagel, 2014).
evidence: This classification is supported by a citation to Isono and Nagel, 2014.

claim: UBPs are the largest group of DUBs.
source: As in yeast and mammals, they can be divided into five classes: the ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolases (UHCs), JAB1/MPN/MOV34 (JAMM) domain DUBs that are zinc metalloproteases, ovarian tumor proteases, the Machado-Josephin domain (MJD) DUBs, and the ubiquitin binding proteins (UBPs), which is the largest group (Isono and Nagel, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Isono and Nagel, 2014.

claim: All UBPs contain specific catalytic Cys- and His-boxes, which are highly conserved in both sequence and length.
source: All UBPs contain specific catalytic Cys- and His-boxes, which are highly conserved in both sequence and length (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2017.

claim: The 27 UBP members can be further divided into 14 subfamilies based on their sequence homology and protein domain organization.
source: Based on their sequence homology and protein domain organization, these 27 members can be further divided into 14 subfamilies (Yan et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2000.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 are the largest UBPs and contain a unique meprin and TRAF homology (MATH) domain.
source: UBP12 and UBP13 are the largest UBPs and contain a unique meprin and TRAF homology (MATH) domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 were first reported to be functional deubiquitinating enzymes that negatively regulate plant immunity.
source: They were first reported to be functional deubiquitinating enzymes that negatively regulate plant immunity (Ewan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ewan et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations in UBP12 and UBP13 result in early flowering and a decreased periodicity of circadian rhythm.
source: Mutations in UBP12 and UBP13 result in early flowering and a decreased periodicity of circadian rhythm (Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claim: GIGANTEA (GI) recruits UBP12 and UBP13 to the ZEITLUPE (ZTL) photoreceptor complex, which antagonizes the E3 ligase activity of ZTL and stabilizes GI, ZTL and TOC1 protein levels.
source: Molecularly, GIGANTEA (GI) recruits UBP12 and UBP13 to the ZEITLUPE (ZTL) photoreceptor complex, which antagonizes the E3 ligase activity of ZTL and hereby stabilizes GI, ZTL and TOC1 [TIMING OF CAB (CHLOROPHYLL A/B-BINDING PROTEIN EXPRESSION) 1] protein levels (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2019.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 can regulate the expression of several genes by deubiquitinating ubiquitinated H2A (H2Aub) upon associating with LIKE HETEROCHROMATIN PROTEIN 1.
source: In addition, UBP12 and UBP13 can regulate the expression of several genes by deubiquitinating ubiquitinated H2A (H2Aub) upon associating with LIKE HETEROCHROMATIN PROTEIN 1, a plant-specific polycomb group (PcG) protein (Derkacheva et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Derkacheva et al., 2016.

claim: Polyubiquitination of MYC2 by the PUB10 E3 ligase can be counteracted by UBP12 and UBP13, preventing degradation of MYC2 by the 26S proteasome which then activates jasmonic acid signaling.
source: Polyubiquitination of MYC2 by the PUB10 E3 ligase can be counteracted by UBP12 and UBP13, preventing degradation of MYC2 by the 26S proteasome which then activates jasmonic acid signaling (Jeong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeong et al., 2017.

claim: ROOT GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR 1 (RGFR1) and ORESARA 1 (ORE1) are deubiquitinated and stabilized by UBP12 and UBP13.
source: In a similar manner, ROOT GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR 1 (RGFR1) and ORESARA 1 (ORE1) are deubiquitinated and therefore stabilized by UBP12 and UBP13, leading to an increased root sensitivity to the RGF1 peptide hormone (An et al., 2018) and an acceleration in leaf senescence (Park et al., 2019), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to An et al., 2018 and Park et al., 2019.

claim: Mutations in UBP12 or UBP13 decrease rosette leaf number and double mutants display severe developmental defects.
source: Mutations in UBP12 or UBP13 decrease rosette leaf number and double mutants display severe developmental defects (Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 interact with DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 in vivo.
source: Here, we found that UBP12 and UBP13 interact with DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by IP-MS/MS data in Figure 1A-C, in vitro pull-down in Figure 1D-F, and in vivo pull-down in Figure 1G.

claim: DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 negatively regulate leaf growth.
source: DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 have previously been documented to negatively regulate leaf growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Upon multiple mono-ubiquitination by BIG BROTHER (BB) or DA2, DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 are activated to cleave growth regulators, such as UBP15, TCP14, TCP15 and TCP22.
source: Upon multiple mono-ubiquitination by BIG BROTHER (BB) or DA2, these latent peptidases are activated to cleave growth regulators, such as UBP15, TCP14, TCP15 and TCP22 (Dong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2017.

claim: The activating E3 ligases BB and DA2 are cleaved and BB is subsequently degraded by the N-degron pathway, mediated by PROTEOLYSIS 1 (PRT1).
source: In addition, the activating E3 ligases BB and DA2 are cleaved and BB is subsequently degraded by the N-degron pathway, mediated by PROTEOLYSIS 1 (PRT1) (Dong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2017.

claim: Single knock-outs in DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 only have very subtle effects on organ size.
source: Single knock-outs in DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 only have very subtle effects on organ size (Dong et al., 2017; Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2017 and Li et al., 2008.

claim: Plant growth is strongly enhanced in the double mutant da1ko_dar1-1, comparable to da1-1 mutants.
source: Plant growth is however strongly enhanced in the double mutant da1ko_dar1-1, comparable to da1-1 mutants, which carry a point mutation (DA1R358K) (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2008.

claim: The DA1R358K mutation has a dominant-negative action towards DA1 and DAR1.
source: The latter mutation has a dominant-negative action towards DA1 and DAR1 (Li et al., 2008) and causes a reduction in peptidase activity (Dong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2008 and Dong et al., 2017.

claim: The DA1R358K mutation causes a reduction in peptidase activity.
source: The latter mutation has a dominant-negative action towards DA1 and DAR1 (Li et al., 2008) and causes a reduction in peptidase activity (Dong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2017.

claim: Rosette growth is severely impaired in the triple mutant da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1, and the size of leaf cells and the extent of endoreduplication are reduced.
source: Rosette growth is however severely impaired in the triple mutant da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1, and the size of leaf cells and the extent of endoreduplication are reduced (Peng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peng et al., 2015.

claim: The da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 phenotype can be complemented by ectopic expression of DA1, DAR1 or DAR2, suggesting they work redundantly in leaves.
source: This phenotype can be complemented by ectopic expression of DA1, DAR1 or DAR2, suggesting they work redundantly in leaves (Peng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peng et al., 2015.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-DA1 results in smaller organs with fewer cells.
source: On the other hand, overexpression of GFP-DA1 results in smaller organs with fewer cells (Vanhaeren et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vanhaeren et al., 2017.

claim: Mutants of UBP15 can abolish the da1-1 phenotype and give rise to smaller organs.
source: Mutants of UBP15 can abolish the da1-1 phenotype and give rise to smaller organs (Du et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Du et al., 2014.

claim: Ectopic expression of UBP15 enhances growth.
source: Inversely, ectopic expression of UBP15 enhances growth (Du et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Du et al., 2014 and Liu et al., 2008.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 not only bind DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, but can also remove ubiquitin from these proteins, rendering them in an inactive state.
source: Here, we demonstrate that UBP12 and UBP13 not only bind DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, but can also remove ubiquitin from these proteins, rendering them in an inactive state.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 were not found to be proteolytically cleaved by DA1, DAR1 or DAR2.
source: Moreover, UBP12 and UBP13 were not found to be proteolytically cleaved by DA1, DAR1 or DAR2, indicating they work upstream in this pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cleaving assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 mutants and overexpression lines exhibit macroscopic, cellular and molecular phenotypes overlapping with those of 35S::GFP-DA1 overexpression lines and da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 mutants.
source: In line with these findings, UBP12 and UBP13 mutants and overexpression lines exhibit macroscopic, cellular and molecular phenotypes overlapping with those of 35S::GFP-DA1 overexpression lines and da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 mutants, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Label free quantification identified a significant enrichment (p-value<0.01) of UBP12 and UBP13 in the GFP-DA1 and GFP-DAR1 samples.
source: Label free quantification identified a significant enrichment (p-value<0.01) of the UBIQUITIN-SPECIFIC PROTEASE 12 (UBP12) and UBP13 in the GFP-DA1 and GFP-DAR1 samples (Figure 1A–B) among other interaction candidates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by IP-MS/MS data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: UBP12 was significantly enriched at a less stringent threshold (p-value<0.05) and UBP13 at the border of significance in GFP-DAR2 samples.
source: Despite the much lower levels of DAR2 MS/MS counts and a lower DAR2 bait protein coverage (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3), we found a significant enrichment of UBP12 at a less stringent threshold (p-value<0.05) and UBP13 at the border of significance (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by IP-MS/MS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HIS-MBP-DA1, HIS-MBP-DAR1 and HIS-MBP-DAR2 could be co-purified with either GST-UBP12 or GST-UBP13, but not with free GST in in vitro pull-down assays.
source: Western blot analysis after purification with anti-GST beads showed that HIS-MBP-DA1, HIS-MBP-DAR1 and HIS-MBP-DAR2 could be co-purified with either GST-UBP12 or GST-UBP13, but not with free GST (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro pull-down data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The interaction between GFP-UBP12 and RFP-DA1, RFP-DAR1 or RFP-DAR2 was confirmed in Arabidopsis cell suspension cultures.
source: Additionally, we co-expressed RFP-DA1, RFP-DAR1 and RFP-DAR2 with either GFP-UBP12 or free GFP from the same vector in Arabidopsis cell suspension cultures. Again, we could confirm the interaction between GFP-UBP12 and RFP-DA1, RFP-DAR1 or RFP-DAR2 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo pull-down data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Both UBP12 and UBP13 are highly and evenly expressed throughout leaf development at comparable levels.
source: Both UBP12 and UBP13 are highly and evenly expressed throughout leaf development at comparable levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 are expressed during leaf development, albeit DAR2 at a lower level.
source: Also DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 are expressed during leaf development as demonstrated before (Peng et al., 2015), albeit DAR2 at a lower level (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and a citation to Peng et al., 2015.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 are localized in the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: Previous research showed that UBP12 and UBP13 are localized in the nucleus and cytoplasm (Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claim: GFP-UBP12 and GFP-UBP13 co-localize in the cytoplasm and the nucleus with RFP-DA1, RFP-DAR1 and RFP-DAR2 in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves.
source: Additional transient expression of GFP-UBP12 or GFP-UBP13 in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves demonstrated that these proteins co-localize in the cytoplasm and the nucleus with RFP-DA1, RFP-DAR1 and RFP-DAR2 (Figure 1—figure supplements 5–10).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 5–10.

claim: All overexpression lines of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 showed a reduction in rosette area.
source: All overexpression lines showed a reduction in rosette area (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Leaves of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 plants appeared to be rounder than those of Col-0.
source: In addition, leaves appeared to be rounder than those of Col-0, a phenotype that can also be observed in da1-1 plants, and the petioles were found to be shorter.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic observations and leaf blade index measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The petioles of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 plants were found to be shorter than those of Col-0.
source: In addition, leaves appeared to be rounder than those of Col-0, a phenotype that can also be observed in da1-1 plants, and the petioles were found to be shorter.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic observations.

claim: da1-1 mutants have a significantly lower leaf blade index compared to Col-0.
source: We could observe a significantly lower leaf blade index in da1-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and in two independent 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines compared to Col-0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), meaning the leaves had a rounder shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by leaf blade index measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two independent 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines have a significantly lower leaf blade index compared to Col-0.
source: We could observe a significantly lower leaf blade index in da1-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and in two independent 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines compared to Col-0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), meaning the leaves had a rounder shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by leaf blade index measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Homozygous plants of several 35S::UBP13 lines were stunted in growth and failed to produce a flower stalk and seeds.
source: For several 35S::UBP13 lines, we were unable to produce stable seed stocks because the homozygous plants were stunted in growth (Figure 2A) and failed to produce a flower stalk and seeds.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ubp12-2 mutant showed a decrease in leaf area.
source: After leaf area measurements, we could observe a decrease in leaf area in the ubp12-2 mutants (Figure 2B), in which the levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 transcripts were previously shown to be downregulated (Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by leaf area measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In ubp12-2 mutants, the levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 transcripts are downregulated.
source: After leaf area measurements, we could observe a decrease in leaf area in the ubp12-2 mutants (Figure 2B), in which the levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 transcripts were previously shown to be downregulated (Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claim: Mutant lines in which only the expression of either UBP12 or UBP13 was downregulated displayed no differences in leaf size compared to the control.
source: Mutant lines in which only the expression of either UBP12 or UBP13 was downregulated, displayed no differences in leaf size compared to the control (Figure 2—figure supplements 4–7).
evidence: This claim is supported by leaf area measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 4–7.

claim: In all UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines, the significant decrease in leaf area was caused by a strong reduction in cell area.
source: In all overexpression lines, the significant decrease in leaf area (29%, 26%, 33% and 36% for 35S::UBP12_3.1, 35S::UBP12_3.2, 35S::UBP13_1.1 and 35S::UBP13_2.3, respectively) was caused by a strong reduction in cell area (26%, 40%, 24% and 46% for 35S::UBP12_3.1, 35S::UBP12_3.2, 35S::UBP13_1.1 and 35S::UBP13_2.3, respectively), whereas the decrease in ubp12-2 leaf size (32%) resulted from a reduction in cell area (21%) and cell number (11%) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cellular analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The decrease in ubp12-2 leaf size resulted from a reduction in cell area and cell number.
source: In all overexpression lines, the significant decrease in leaf area (29%, 26%, 33% and 36% for 35S::UBP12_3.1, 35S::UBP12_3.2, 35S::UBP13_1.1 and 35S::UBP13_2.3, respectively) was caused by a strong reduction in cell area (26%, 40%, 24% and 46% for 35S::UBP12_3.1, 35S::UBP12_3.2, 35S::UBP13_1.1 and 35S::UBP13_2.3, respectively), whereas the decrease in ubp12-2 leaf size (32%) resulted from a reduction in cell area (21%) and cell number (11%) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cellular analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines harbored a larger proportion of very small cells in addition to a general decrease in mature pavement cell size.
source: A cell area distribution plot confirmed that indeed all independent UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines harbored a larger proportion of these small cells in addition to a general decrease in mature pavement cell size (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell area distribution data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: For the ubp12-2 mutant, no differences in cell area distribution compared to Col-0 could be observed.
source: For the ubp12-2 mutant, no differences in cell area distribution compared to Col-0 could be observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell area distribution data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 10.

claim: At nine days after stratification (DAS), all leaf cells of Col-0, 35S::UBP12_3.1 and 35S::UBP13_1.1 exhibited a 2C or 4C content, demonstrating the majority of cells are still in the mitotic cell cycle.
source: At nine days after stratification (DAS), all leaf cells of the three lines exhibited a 2C or 4C content, demonstrating the majority of cells are still in the mitotic cell cycle (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: From 12 DAS onwards, cells with 8C started to appear, indicating the onset of endoreduplication.
source: From 12 DAS onwards, cells with 8C started to appear, indicating the onset of endoreduplication.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 12 DAS, leaves of 35S::UBP12 plants contained a significantly larger proportion of 2C cells (53%) than those of the Col-0 (43%) and a significantly lower amount of 4C cells (44% and 52%, respectively).
source: At 12 DAS, leaves of 35S::UBP12 plants contained a significantly larger proportion of 2 C cells (53%) than those of the Col-0 (43%) and a significantly lower amount of 4 C cells (44% and 52%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 15 DAS, the amount of 8C nuclei was significantly lower in 35S::UBP12 (28%) than in the control (35%).
source: At 15 DAS, the amount of 8C nuclei was significantly lower in 35S::UBP12 (28%) than in the control (35%) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 35S::UBP13 leaves had a significantly higher amount of 2C cells at 12 DAS (61%) and 15 DAS (42%) compared to Col-0 (43% and 25%, respectively).
source: Similar, but more pronounced observations were found in 35S::UBP13 leaves, in which a significantly higher amount of 2 C cells was detected at 12 DAS (61%) and 15 DAS (42%) compared to Col-0 (43% and 25%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 35S::UBP13 leaves had a lower level of 4C cells at 12 DAS (35%) compared to Col-0 (52%).
source: In addition, a lower level of 4 C cells was found at 12 DAS (35% in 35S::UBP13, 52% in Col-0) and fewer cells with 8C were present at 15, 18, 21 and 27 DAS in 35S::UBP13 (22%, 33%, 35% and 35%, respectively) compared to Col-0 (35%, 42%, 42% and 46%, respectively) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fewer cells with 8C were present at 15, 18, 21 and 27 DAS in 35S::UBP13 (22%, 33%, 35% and 35%, respectively) compared to Col-0 (35%, 42%, 42% and 46%, respectively).
source: In addition, a lower level of 4 C cells was found at 12 DAS (35% in 35S::UBP13, 52% in Col-0) and fewer cells with 8C were present at 15, 18, 21 and 27 DAS in 35S::UBP13 (22%, 33%, 35% and 35%, respectively) compared to Col-0 (35%, 42%, 42% and 46%, respectively) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 9 DAS, there was a significantly higher expression of ANT, GRF5 and KLUH in 35S::UBP13 lines compared to the Col-0.
source: At 9 DAS, when all epidermal cells are actively dividing (Andriankaja et al., 2012), we could observe a significantly higher expression of ANT, GRF5 and KLUH in 35S::UBP13 lines compared to the Col-0 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 12 DAS, there was a significant higher expression of AN3 and GRF5 and the cell division marker CYCB1;1 in 35S::UBP13 leaves.
source: Later in development at 12 DAS, a large portion of the Col-0 cells should have exited the mitotic division cycle and start to differentiate (Andriankaja et al., 2012; Donnelly et al., 1999; Kazama et al., 2010). Still, there was a significant higher expression of AN3 and GRF5 and the cell division marker CYCB1;1 in 35S::UBP13 leaves (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: On 15 DAS, the expression levels of ANT and CYCB1;1 were elevated in 35S::UBP13 leaves.
source: On 15 DAS, the expression levels of ANT and CYCB1;one were elevated in 35S::UBP13 leaves (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and finally, at 18 DAS, ANT was still significantly higher expressed in 35S::UBP13 compared to the Col-0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: At 18 DAS, ANT was still significantly higher expressed in 35S::UBP13 compared to the Col-0.
source: On 15 DAS, the expression levels of ANT and CYCB1;one were elevated in 35S::UBP13 leaves (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and finally, at 18 DAS, ANT was still significantly higher expressed in 35S::UBP13 compared to the Col-0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: In Col-0 leaf tips at 12 DAS, the epidermal cells had started to expand and differentiate.
source: To further explore these observations, we characterized the epidermal cells of tips of the third leaf of 12 day old seedlings, which should be undergoing cell differentiation at this stage in Col-0 (Andriankaja et al., 2012). In Col-0 leaf tips, we could indeed observe that the epidermal cells had started to expand and differentiate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Similar leaf tips of 35S::UBP12 or 35S::UBP13 plants at 12 DAS contained almost exclusively undifferentiated cells.
source: On the contrary, similar leaf tips of 35S::UBP12 or 35S::UBP13 plants contained almost exclusively undifferentiated cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cell number was not significantly altered in UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines.
source: These results, together with our observation that cell number was not significantly altered in UBP12 an UBP13 overexpression lines, indicate that especially during the early developmental stages of leaf growth, endoreduplication and cell differentiation are delayed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves.
evidence: This claim is supported by cellular analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Endoreduplication and cell differentiation are delayed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves during the early developmental stages of leaf growth.
source: These results, together with our observation that cell number was not significantly altered in UBP12 an UBP13 overexpression lines, indicate that especially during the early developmental stages of leaf growth, endoreduplication and cell differentiation are delayed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including ploidy analysis, gene expression data, and cellular imaging.

claim: Ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 can be deubiquitinated by GST-UBP12 or GST-UBP13, but their respective catalytic mutants fail to do so.
source: Figure 4A shows that ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 can be deubiquitinated by GST-UBP12 or GST-UBP13, but their respective catalytic mutants fail to do so.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Similar deubiquitination activities could be observed for the substrates DAR1 and DAR2.
source: Similar deubiquitination activities could be observed for the substrates DAR1 and DAR2 (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Both GST-UBP12 and GST-UBP13 could strongly deubiquitinate HIS-MBP-DA1, but no such effect could be observed upon addition of GST-UBP3, GST-UBP15 or GST-UBP24.
source: We found again that both GST-UBP12 and GST-UBP13 could strongly deubiquitinate HIS-MBP-DA1, but no such effect could be observed upon addition of GST-UBP3, GST-UBP15 or GST-UBP24 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: After 1 hr, a shift in molecular weight occurred in the ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 samples that were incubated with Col-0 extract, and this shift did not occur in the sample that was incubated with the ubp12-2 extract.
source: Already after 1 hr, we could observe a shift in molecular weight in the ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 samples that were incubated with Col-0 extract (Figure 5A), and this shift did not occur in the sample that was incubated with the ubp12-2 extract (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The intensity of ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 bands faded faster in the presence of Col-0 extract than in the presence of ubp12-2 extract.
source: In addition, the intensity of ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 bands faded faster in the presence of Col-0 extract than in the presence of ubp12-2 extract (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: When ubiquitinated DA1 proteins were incubated with equal extracts of 35S::UBP12 or 35S::UBP13 plants, the intensity of ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 disappeared at a faster rate.
source: In addition, when ubiquitinated DA1 proteins were incubated with equal extracts of 35S::UBP12 (Figure 5F) or 35S::UBP13 (Figure 5G) plants, the intensity of ubiquitinated HIS-MBP-DA1 disappeared at a faster rate (Figure 5D–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-free deubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5D-H.

claim: No increases in protein abundance were identified in the 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP12 and 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP13 samples compared to those of 35S::GFP-DA1.
source: In addition, we extracted proteins of 35S::GFP-DA1, 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP12 and 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP13 plants and performed a purification with anti-GFP beads from equal protein inputs. After purification, we submitted the samples to Western Blot and detected the abundance of GFP-DA1 proteins. We could not identify increases in protein abundance in the 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP12 and 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP13 samples compared to those of 35S::GFP-DA1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting UBP12 and UBP13 do not prevent potential removal of polyubiquitination of DA1 and hereby prevent its degradation by the proteasome.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 do not prevent potential removal of polyubiquitination of DA1 and hereby prevent its degradation by the proteasome.
source: We could not identify increases in protein abundance in the 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP12 and 35S::GFP-DA1_35S::UBP13 samples compared to those of 35S::GFP-DA1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting UBP12 and UBP13 do not prevent potential removal of polyubiquitination of DA1 and hereby prevent its degradation by the proteasome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 4 hr of incubation, the intensities of all GST-tagged UBP proteins were equal and no additional cleaving fragments could be observed in the HIS-MBP-DA1 samples compared to those with HIS-MBP-DA1H418A,H422A.
source: However, after 4 hr of incubation, the intensities of all GST-tagged UBP proteins were equal and no additional cleaving fragments could be observed in the HIS-MBP-DA1 samples compared to those with HIS-MBP-DA1H418A,H422A (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cleaving assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In all double overexpression lines of 35S::GFP-DA1 and 35S::UBP12 or 35S::UBP13, similar phenotypes as in the 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines in the Col-0 background were observed.
source: In all double overexpression lines, we could observe similar phenotypes as in the 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines in the Col-0 background (Figure 6B, Figure 2A), suggesting that the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression phenotype is dominant and UBP12 and UBP13 are not destabilized by DA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 2A.

claim: The UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression phenotype is dominant.
source: In all double overexpression lines, we could observe similar phenotypes as in the 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines in the Col-0 background (Figure 6B, Figure 2A), suggesting that the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression phenotype is dominant and UBP12 and UBP13 are not destabilized by DA1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genetic analysis of double overexpression lines.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 are not destabilized by DA1.
source: In all double overexpression lines, we could observe similar phenotypes as in the 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 lines in the Col-0 background (Figure 6B, Figure 2A), suggesting that the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression phenotype is dominant and UBP12 and UBP13 are not destabilized by DA1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genetic analysis of double overexpression lines.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 act upstream of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 to counteract their ubiquitination.
source: Thus, our biochemical, genetic and phenotypic analyses show that UBP12 and UBP13 are not cleavage substrates, but act upstream of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 to counteract their ubiquitination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including deubiquitination assays, cleaving assays, and genetic analyses.

claim: By limiting their peptidase activity, UBP12 and UBP13 fine-tune leaf growth, cell size and endoreduplication.
source: By limiting their peptidase activity, UBP12 and UBP13 fine-tune leaf growth, cell size and endoreduplication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including phenotypic, cellular, and molecular analyses.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 work antagonistically to BB and DA2.
source: In this study, we identified two ubiquitin-specific proteases, UBP12 an UBP13, that interact with DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 in vitro and in vivo. Our experiments demonstrate that these UBPs work antagonistically to BB and DA2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from deubiquitination assays and genetic analyses.

claim: Incubation of ubiquitinated DA1, DAR1 or DAR2 with either UBP12 or UBP13 resulted in strong deubiquitination.
source: Incubation of ubiquitinated DA1, DAR1 or DAR2 with either UBP12 or UBP13 resulted in strong deubiquitination.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 can also interact with the unubiquitinated forms of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2.
source: Interestingly, our in vitro immunoprecipitation (IP) shows that UBP12 and UBP13 can also interact with the unubiquitinated forms of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro pull-down data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: UBP15 has no deubiquitination activity towards DA1.
source: Our results indicate that UBP15 has no deubiquitination activity towards DA1 and acts therefore downstream in this pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: UBP15 acts downstream in the DA1 pathway.
source: Our results indicate that UBP15 has no deubiquitination activity towards DA1 and acts therefore downstream in this pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from deubiquitination assays and prior knowledge about UBP15 being a cleavage substrate of DA1.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 have recently been described to deubiquitinate various poly-ubiquitinated proteins, preventing their proteasomal degradation.
source: UBP12 and UBP13 have recently been described to deubiquitinate various poly-ubiquitinated proteins, preventing their proteasomal degradation (An et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to An et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 can decrease the levels of mono-ubiquitinated H2A.
source: In addition, they can decrease the levels of mono-ubiquitinated H2A (Derkacheva et al., 2016) and remove multiple mono-ubiquitinations from DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 as described here.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Derkacheva et al., 2016.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 remove multiple mono-ubiquitinations from DA1, DAR1 and DAR2.
source: In addition, they can decrease the levels of mono-ubiquitinated H2A (Derkacheva et al., 2016) and remove multiple mono-ubiquitinations from DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 as described here.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 demonstrate flexibility towards different types of ubiquitination.
source: This demonstrates the flexibility of these UBPs towards different types of ubiquitination (Clague et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that UBP12 and UBP13 can deubiquitinate both poly-ubiquitinated proteins and multiple mono-ubiquitinated proteins.

claim: No evidence was found that besides the removal of the multiple mono-ubiquitination sites of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, potential degradation of these proteins by removal of poly-ubiquitination was mediated by UBP12 or UBP13.
source: Here, we could not find evidence that besides the removal of the multiple mono-ubiquitination sites of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, potential degradation of these proteins by removal of poly-ubiquitination was mediated by UBP12 or UBP13.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Downregulation of either UBP12 or UBP13 did not alter leaf size, indicating that these genes work redundantly in controlling leaf size.
source: In contrast to the early flowering time-related genes (Cui et al., 2013), downregulation of either UBP12 or UBP13 did not alter leaf size, indicating that these genes work redundantly in controlling leaf size.
evidence: This claim is supported by leaf area measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 4–7.

claim: The leaf area was only reduced in ubp12-2 mutants, in which levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 are decreased.
source: The leaf area was only reduced in ubp12-2 mutants, in which levels of both UBP12 and UBP13 are decreased (Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by leaf area measurements shown in Figure 2B and a citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claim: The decreased deubiquitination activity towards DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 could result in an accumulation of the activated peptidases in ubp12-2 mutants, leading to a decrease in cell number and leaf area.
source: The subsequently decreased deubiquitination activity towards DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 could result in an accumulation of the activated peptidases in ubp12-2 mutants, leading to a decrease in cell number and leaf area.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the phenotypic data.

claim: A similar phenotype to ubp12-2 is also observed in GFP-DA1 overexpressing plants and in the ubp15 mutant.
source: A similar phenotype is also observed in GFP-DA1 overexpressing plants (Vanhaeren et al., 2017) and in the ubp15 mutant (Du et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vanhaeren et al., 2017; Du et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2008.

claim: High ectopic expression of either UBP12 or UBP13 would result in very low levels of ubiquitinated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, leading to a severe disturbance of leaf development.
source: In contrast, high ectopic expression of either UBP12 or UBP13 would result in very low levels of ubiquitinated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, leading to a severe disturbance of leaf development.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the phenotypic data.

claim: 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 plants were strongly reduced in growth in a similar manner as da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 triple mutants.
source: Indeed, 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 plants were strongly reduced in growth in a similar manner as da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 triple mutants (Peng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 2A and a citation to Peng et al., 2015.

claim: A more detailed cellular and molecular analysis of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves revealed a strong reduction in cell area and a decrease in ploidy levels at the early stages of leaf development, which were also observed in da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 plants.
source: A more detailed cellular and molecular analysis of 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 leaves revealed more parallels, such as a strong reduction in cell area and a decrease in ploidy levels at the early stages of leaf development, which were also observed in da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 plants (Peng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by cellular and ploidy data shown in Figures 2 and 3, and a citation to Peng et al., 2015.

claim: The complete absence of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 proteins in da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 plants could explain its stronger reduction in endoreduplication than that of UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines.
source: The complete absence of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 proteins in da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 plants could however explain its stronger reduction in endoreduplication than that of UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines, in which ubiquitination of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 can still occur, but is likely kept at a very low level.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation comparing the phenotypes of different genotypes.

claim: Several markers of cell proliferation were found to be more highly expressed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 during early stages of leaf development, similarly as observed in plants that contain a DA1R358K mutation.
source: In addition, several markers of cell proliferation were found to be more highly expressed in 35S::UBP12 and 35S::UBP13 during early stages of leaf development, similarly as observed in plants that contain a DA1R358K mutation (Vanhaeren et al., 2017), which reduces the peptidase activity of DA1 (Dong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B-C and citations to Vanhaeren et al., 2017 and Dong et al., 2017.

claim: The final cell number in the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines was not increased, suggesting that a strong reduction of DA1 activity rather delays development but does not increase the duration of cell proliferation and hence the final number of cells.
source: However, the final cell number in the UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines was not increased, suggesting that a strong reduction of DA1 activity rather delays development but does not increase the duration of cell proliferation and hence the final number of cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from cellular analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 negatively regulate their own activity by cleaving their activating E3-ligases BB and DA2, resulting in an activation-repression system.
source: Previously, it has been shown that DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 negatively regulate their own activity by cleaving their activating E3-ligases BB and DA2, resulting in an activation-repression system (Dong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2017.

claim: UBP12 and UBP13 form an additional layer of post-translational regulation to limit the activity of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 by specifically removing ubiquitin.
source: UBP12 and UBP13 form an additional layer of post-translational regulation to limit the activity of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 by specifically removing ubiquitin, and hence further fine-tune organ growth in this growth-regulatory pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: This dual system to limit and fine-tune the activity of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 demonstrates the importance of keeping a correct balance between the active and inactive pool of these proteases during leaf development.
source: This dual system to limit and fine-tune the activity of DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 demonstrates the importance of keeping a correct balance between the active and inactive pool of these proteases during leaf development.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: In wild-type conditions, a correct balance between an inactive and active (ubiquitinated) DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 results in an intact exit from mitosis and standard ploidy levels in leaf cells, which leads to normal plant growth.
source: In wild-type conditions, a correct balance between an inactive and active (ubiquitinated) DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 results in an intact exit from mitosis and standard ploidy levels in leaf cells, which leads to normal plant growth (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a model summarizing the findings, illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: High levels of UBP12 or UBP13 can shift the balance to a depletion of activated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, which results in a delayed endoreduplication, a severe reduction in cell size and stunted plant growth.
source: High levels of UBP12 or UBP13 can however shift the balance to a depletion of activated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, which results in a delayed endoreduplication, a severe reduction in cell size and stunted plant growth (Figure 7B), which is highly similar to the phenotype of da1ko_dar1-1_dar2-1 mutants (Peng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a model summarizing the findings, illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: Low levels of UBP12 and UBP13 might lead to an increase in activated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 levels, more destabilization of its substrates and can hence limit plant growth by reducing both cell area and cell number.
source: Low levels of UBP12 and UBP13 might on the other hand lead to an increase in activated DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 levels, more destabilization of its substrates and can hence limit plant growth by reducing both cell area and cell number (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a model summarizing the findings, illustrated in Figure 7C.

claim: Both very low and high levels of DA1 result in growth reduction.
source: Because both very low and high levels of DA1 result in growth reduction (Peng et al., 2015; Vanhaeren et al., 2017), a tight balance between active and inactive DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 is crucial for normal plant development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2015 and Vanhaeren et al., 2017.

claim: A tight balance between active and inactive DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 is crucial for normal plant development.
source: Because both very low and high levels of DA1 result in growth reduction (Peng et al., 2015; Vanhaeren et al., 2017), a tight balance between active and inactive DA1, DAR1 and DAR2 is crucial for normal plant development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and prior literature.

claim: With UBP12 and UBP13 expression levels being relatively constant throughout leaf development, unknown post-translational modifications of UBP12 and UBP13 are likely to alter the activity or specificity towards DA1, DAR1 and DAR2.
source: With UBP12 and UBP13 expression levels being relatively constant throughout leaf development, unknown post-translational modifications of UBP12 and UBP13 are likely to alter the activity or specificity towards DA1, DAR1 and DAR2, as is the case with other deubiquitinating enzymes (Huang and Cochran, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation of constant expression levels and knowledge about other DUBs.

claim: It remains unclear if the reduction in cell area in the ubp12-2 mutants or UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines results only from altered levels of DA1 activity, or if UBP12 and UBP13 regulate cell expansion through other growth regulators.
source: Additionally, it remains also unclear if this reduction in cell area in the ubp12-2 mutants or UBP12 and UBP13 overexpression lines results only from altered levels of DA1 activity, or if UBP12 and UBP13 regulate cell expansion through other growth regulators.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study.
